candidates.title: A Prospective Randomized Trial to Assess Early versus Delayed Weight Bearing Following Operatively Treated Ankle Fractures in the United States.
candidates.authors_short: Obremskey WT, Archer KR, et al.
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To determine the safety of early versus delayed weight bearing and effectiveness for improving return-to-work following ankle fracture repair. METHODS: Design: Prospective randomized study. SETTING: 19 United States Trauma Centers. PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Adult patients (≥18 years) with ankle fracture (OTA/AO 44 A, B or C) undergoing surgical fixation were included. Open Gustilo-Anderson (G-A) Type IIIB, IIIC, syndesmotic injuries with fixation, and injuries with arterial impaction that surgeons felt unsafe to weight were excluded. OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: The co-primary outcomes were (1) non-inferiority of early versus delayed weight bearing for reoperation for complications of hardware failure, non-union, loss of reduction, infection, or fusion; and (2) gated superiority of early versus delayed weight bearing for time to return-to-work, both within 365 days of randomization. Reoperation and time to return-to-work was compared between patients assigned to early (2 weeks post-operatively) versus delayed (6 weeks post-operatively) weight bearing. RESULTS: The modified intent to treat sample included 418 patients enrolled between January 2020 through October 2023; 214 early (mean age: 47; SD (15) range (18-84); 35% male); 204 delayed (mean age: 43; SD (15); 36% male). Reoperation for complication occurred in 5 early (2.3%, 95% Confidence Interval (CI): 0.3%, 4.4%), and 7 delayed patients (3.4%, 95% CI: 0.9%, 5.9%). Median time to return-to-work (95% CI) was 54 (42, 77) days and 69 (47, 89) days for the early and delayed groups, respectively. Early weight bearing was non-inferior to delayed weight bearing for reoperation (difference in complication free survival (early - delayed): 1.5 percentage points; 90% two sided CI: -1.7%, 4.8% which excluded the non-inferiority tolerance of -5.0%) and not superior for return-to-work (Hazard Ratio 1.1, 95% CI: 0.8, 1.6, p=0.475). CONCLUSIONS: Trial findings add to the growing evidence demonstrating the safety of early weight bearing after fixation of bimalleolar and trimalleolar ankle fracture without syndesmotic disruption, a key concern for both clinicians and patients. However, no statistically significant benefit of earlier return-to-work was found. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: I.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large multicenter RCT from 19 US trauma centers (n=418) with co-primary outcomes addressing a highly clinically relevant question about early versus delayed weight bearing after operative ankle fracture fixation, published in a respected trauma journal.
bullets: Early weight bearing at 2 weeks after operative ankle fracture fixation carries the same low reoperation risk as delayed weight bearing at 6 weeks, in patients without syndesmotic injury.
These findings apply to adults with bimalleolar or trimalleolar ankle fractures fixed at a trauma center, excluding open IIIB/IIIC injuries and those requiring syndesmotic fixation.
Surgeons can allow weight bearing at 2 weeks post-fixation without increasing complications, though patients should not expect a significantly faster return to work.

candidates.title: To Walk or Not? A Prospective, Randomised Controlled Trial to Evaluate the Effect of Weightbearing on Patient Outcomes Following First Metatarsophalangeal Joint Fusion.
candidates.authors_short: Purdie SD, Glazebrook HM, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: First metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint arthrodesis is the gold standard surgical treatment of hallux rigidus and severe hallux valgus with osteoarthritis after failed nonoperative management. Despite its common use, postoperative weightbearing protocols vary considerably. To date, no prospective randomised controlled trials have directly compared outcomes between immediate weightbearing as tolerated (WBAT) and non-weightbearing (NWB) using modern fixation techniques. This study aimed to evaluate whether immediate WBAT following first metatarsophalangeal joint arthrodesis leads to differences in patient outcomes compared with traditional non-weightbearing protocols. METHODS: A prospective randomised controlled trial was conducted including 68 patients undergoing isolated first-MTP fusion. Patients were randomly allocated either WBAT or NWB protocols. Standardised surgical technique and fixation (crossed screws or plate) were performed by 2 fellowship-trained foot and ankle surgeons. Primary outcomes were the visual analogue scale (VAS) pain scores and the Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM-activities of daily living [ADL] subscale) functional scores, at 12 months. Secondary outcomes included non-union, complications including infection, wound issues, and patient satisfaction. Statistical analysis used t tests and χ2 or Fisher exact tests, with significance at P < .05. RESULTS: Sixty-eight patients (33 WBAT, 35 NWB) completed follow-up. Both groups demonstrated significant improvements in pain and function at 12 months (P < .001 for both). No statistically significant differences were found between WBAT and NWB groups in VAS pain scores (2.97 ± 2.215 vs 2.54 ± 2.147; P = .423), FAAM scores (81.31 ± 16.028 vs 85.02 ± 18.863; P = .387), or patient satisfaction (8.00 ± 2.76 vs 8.34 ± 2.52; P = .594). Complication rates were comparable, with 1 case of hardware irritation in each group (P = .739). CONCLUSION: Following first-MTP joint fusion, immediate weightbearing is safe and results in similar pain relief, patient satisfaction, and complication rates compared with traditional NWB protocols, although a clinically meaningful functional advantage for NWB could not be excluded. These findings support more permissive postoperative strategies, which may offer benefits for patient mobility, independence, recovery time, and health care resource use that were not directly measured in this trial. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, randomised controlled trial. CLINICALTRIALS: gov ID:NCT04473196.
candidates.score_reasoning: High-quality RCT from JBJS American volume on a landmark comparison of SFA versus ISB for arthroscopic shoulder surgery with direct practice implications for phrenic-nerve-sparing analgesia, reasonable sample size (n=80), and noninferiority design.
bullets: Immediate weightbearing after first MTP fusion produces the same pain relief, function scores, and complication rates at 12 months as traditional non-weightbearing protocols.
This applies to patients undergoing first MTP arthrodesis for hallux rigidus or severe hallux valgus fixed with crossed screws or a plate by a foot and ankle surgeon.
Surgeons can allow immediate weightbearing after first MTP fusion without increasing non-union or complication risk, removing the need for routine postoperative non-weightbearing restrictions.

candidates.title: Lateral Opening-Wedge Versus Medial Closing-Wedge Distal Femoral Osteotomy for Adolescent Idiopathic Genu Valgum: A Randomised Controlled Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Khatri JP, Ghosh AK, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Distal femoral osteotomy is used to correct symptomatic genu valgum after distal femoral physeal closure, but comparative evidence between lateral opening-wedge osteotomy (LOW) and medial closing-wedge osteotomy (MCW) in adolescents is limited. We compared radiographic correction, recovery, and complications between the techniques. METHODS: In this prospective randomised trial, 65 adolescents aged 12 to 18 years with idiopathic genu valgum and radiographic closure of the distal femoral physis were allocated 1:1 to LOW or MCW. Three participants were lost to follow-up, leaving 62 participants for the available-case analysis (LOW, n=32; MCW, n=30). In bilateral cases, only the first operated limb was analyzed. The primary outcome was signed mechanical axis deviation (MAD) at radiographic union; unadjusted comparisons were the primary focus, and covariate-adjusted analyses were supportive. RESULTS: MAD at union was 6.8±6.2 mm after LOW and 2.4±5.3 mm after MCW (LOW minus MCW, 4.4 mm; 95% CI: 1.5-7.3; P=0.003). The supportive adjusted difference was 3.0 mm (95% CI: -0.4 to 6.5; P=0.08). Absolute deviation from neutral was 6.8±6.2 versus 4.0±4.1 mm (difference, 2.8 mm; 95% CI: 0.2-5.5; P=0.04). At union, mLDFA did not differ significantly; aLDFA favored MCW in the unadjusted analysis, but neither adjusted angular difference was significant. One-year Pedi-IKDC scores, pain, satisfaction, union time, hospital stay, and return to activity did not differ between groups. Unique symptomatic lateral plate/iliotibial-band irritation occurred in 4 of 32 LOW participants (13%) and 3 of 30 MCW participants (10%; P=1.00). CONCLUSIONS: MAD at radiographic union favored MCW, but the trial did not establish clinically meaningful superiority. The adjusted estimate was smaller and nonsignificant, and no sustained functional advantage was detected. Both techniques produced substantial correction with favorable short- to mid-term outcomes. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I-therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large propensity-score-matched nationwide database study (n=5,408 matched) in JBJS addressing the clinically important THA versus hemiarthroplasty question in the 65-75 age group for femoral neck fracture, with actionable 90-day readmission findings.
bullets: In adolescents with closed physes and symptomatic genu valgum, medial closing-wedge distal femoral osteotomy achieved slightly better mechanical axis alignment at union than lateral opening-wedge, but the difference was small and lost significance after adjustment.
Functional outcomes, pain, satisfaction, union time, and return to activity were similar between the two techniques at one year.
Either technique is a reasonable choice for this patient group, as both produced reliable correction without a clinically meaningful difference in results or complication rates.

candidates.title: Preoperative Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor Use is Associated With Increased Complication Risk After Total Hip Arthroplasty: A Dose-Response Analysis.
candidates.authors_short: Alfonsi SP, Zickler CL, et al.
candidates.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Preoperative selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) use has been associated with adverse outcomes following primary total hip arthroplasty (THA). This study examined whether complication rates vary based on SSRI daily dosage. METHODS: A claims database (2010 to 2023) identified 77,958 primary THA patients who did not have osteoporosis and who filled an SSRI prescription 60 days preoperatively. Patients were matched 1:3 to SSRI-naive individuals by age, sex, Charlson Comorbidity Index, and history of cognitive disorders, depression, anxiety, and substance use. Overall, 77,958 SSRI users were matched to 233,277 controls (mean age 65 years). After matching, baseline demographics and rates of anxiety and depression (all P > 0.13) were similar between cohorts. The SSRI doses were standardized using quantity, duration, and strength, then stratified as low (0 to 30 mg), medium (30 to 100 mg), or high (greater than 100 mg). Multivariate regression and Kaplan-Meier analysis assessed surgical complications and revision-free survival at 2-year follow-up. RESULTS: Preoperative SSRI use was associated with greater 2-year complications (5.2 versus 3.2%, P < 0.001). In adjusted multivariate analysis, SSRI use was associated with increased odds of component loosening (OR [odds ratio] 1.5), periprosthetic fracture (OR 1.8), periprosthetic joint infection (OR 1.7), dislocation (OR 2.0), and revision surgery (OR 1.7) (all P < 0.001). There was no dose-dependent relationship observed. Component loosening approached statistical significance at high SSRI doses (OR 3.7, P = 0.07). Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated reduced revision-free survival among SSRI users (P < 0.001) at 2-year follow-up. CONCLUSION: Preoperative SSRI use, regardless of dose, was associated with higher 2-year rates of periprosthetic joint infection, dislocation, fracture, loosening, and revision. However, the absence of a dose-response relationship suggests that SSRIs are unlikely to be directly responsible for these complications.
candidates.score_reasoning: Highly clinically relevant RCT (n=65 adolescents) from a pediatric orthopaedics journal directly comparing two distal femoral osteotomy techniques with radiographic and functional outcomes, providing actionable surgical decision-making data.
bullets: THA patients on preoperative SSRIs had twice the rate of major complications at 2 years compared to matched controls, including higher rates of infection, dislocation, fracture, and revision.
The increased risk applied regardless of SSRI dose, suggesting SSRIs are likely a marker of underlying patient vulnerability rather than a direct cause of implant failure.
Orthopaedic surgeons should use preoperative SSRI use as a flag for higher-risk THA patients who may warrant closer postoperative surveillance and optimisation counselling.

candidates.title: Mechanical Failure and Revision Risk Following Transition from PFNA to TFNA: A Single-Center Cohort Study of 1,970 Patients.
candidates.authors_short: Ben Zoor I, Fogel I, et al.
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare implant mechanical failure, cut-out rate, and time to failure between two cephalomedullary nail designs following an institutional transition. METHODS: Design: Retrospective consecutive cohort study. SETTING: Single Level I trauma center, Israel. PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Patients aged >65 years with acute OTA/AO 31A fractures (subtypes 31A1-31A3) treated with a short cephalomedullary nail with helical blade fixation, either the Proximal Femoral Nail Antirotation (PFNA) or the Trochanteric Fixation Nail-Advanced (TFNA), between January 2018 and May 2025 were included. Implant type was determined solely by an institutional transition from PFNA to TFNA in March 2023 for logistical reasons rather than surgeon preference. OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: Implant mechanical failure, cut-out rate, time to failure, body mass index (BMI), and Tip-Apex Distance (TAD) were compared between groups. Mortality within the early revision-risk window was compared between groups to exclude survival bias. RESULTS: The PFNA cohort comprised 1,388 patients (mean age 83.1 years, range 65-102; 986 females [71.0%]) and the TFNA cohort 582 patients (mean age 82.9 years, range 65-107; 407 females [69.9%]); baseline demographics were comparable (age, p=0.691; sex, p=0.626). Orthopedic follow-up was 63.9% for the TFNA cohort versus 61.0% for the PFNA cohort (p=0.24), with a shorter maximum observation period for TFNA (TFNA 26 vs. PFNA 88 months).TFNA was associated with a five-fold increase in implant mechanical failure relative to PFNA (TFNA 1.6% vs. PFNA 0.3%; RR=5.36, 95% CI 1.66-17.3; p=0.005), primarily driven by a four-fold increase in cut-outs (1.2% vs. 0.3%; RR=4.18, 95% CI 1.23-14.2; p=0.027). Failures occurred earlier with TFNA (median 80.0 vs. 244.0 days; p=0.027). Among cut-outs, OTA/AO subtype distribution did not differ (31A1: TFNA 57.1% vs. PFNA 50.0%; no 31A3 in either group; p=1.00); TFNA patients had a higher BMI (median 23.9 vs. 20.1 kg/m 2 ; p=0.024), but mean TAD did not differ (TFNA 24.6 vs. PFNA 21.1 mm; p=0.37). Mortality within the revision-risk window did not differ (TFNA 7.2% vs. PFNA 8.8%; p=0.24). CONCLUSIONS: The transition to the Trochanteric Fixation Nail-Advanced (TFNA) was associated with five-fold higher mechanical failure and four-fold higher cut-out rates than the Proximal Femoral Nail Antirotation (PFNA) with earlier failures suggesting reduced mechanical stability of the TFNA during early fracture healing. Heightened vigilance is warranted when using TFNA, particularly in patients with higher body mass index early postoperatively. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic Level III.
candidates.score_reasoning: Very large claims-based cohort (n=311,235 matched patients) in Journal of Arthroplasty examining dose-response relationship between preoperative SSRI use and THA complications including PJI, dislocation, and revision, with direct preoperative screening implications.
bullets: In 1,970 patients over 65 with hip fractures, the TFNA had a five-fold higher mechanical failure rate and four-fold higher cut-out rate compared to the PFNA (1.6% vs. 0.3%).
Failures with the TFNA occurred much earlier, at a median of 80 days versus 244 days with the PFNA, suggesting the TFNA provides less stability during early fracture healing.
Surgeons using the TFNA should follow patients closely in the first three months after surgery, with extra caution in patients with higher body weight.

candidates.title: Cemented Femoral Fixation for Primary Total Hip Arthroplasty in the United States: How Surgeon-Cemented Volume Impacts Failure Risk.
candidates.authors_short: Abrolat JL, Zedan AM, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Although cementless femoral fixation remains the United States (U.S.) standard, recent data shows a decline in exclusive cementless usage from 34 to 14% between 2018 and 2024. Whether surgeon-cemented total hip arthroplasty (THA) volume affects implant survivorship remains unclear in this traditionally low-volume environment. As such, we evaluated the association between surgeon cemented stem volume and risk of all-cause revision. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study used a national database to identify primary THAs with cemented femoral fixation from 2016 to 2020. Surgeons were classified by their five-year cemented stem volume: Group 1 (less than 60 stems) or Group 2 (≥ 60 stems). Patients had a minimum two-year follow-up and were propensity score-matched 1:1 based on demographics and comorbidities. A total of 7,174 matched patients were analyzed (3,587 per cohort). Outcomes were all-cause revision, periprosthetic fracture (PPF), mechanical loosening, periprosthetic joint infection (PJI), and dislocation within five years. RESULTS: Patients treated by Group 1 surgeons had higher rates of all study outcomes. At two years, Group 1 patients had higher odds of all-cause revision (odds ratio (OR) = 2.10; 95% confidence interval: 1.44 to 3.11; P < 0.001). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed revision risk diverged sharply within the first postoperative year and persisted through five years. At two-year follow-up, Group 1 patients had increased risk of PPF (OR = 1.58; P = 0.038), loosening (OR = 2.21; P < 0.001), PJI (OR = 2.19; P < 0.001), and dislocation (OR = 2.51; P < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Low surgeon cemented stem volume is strongly associated with increased risk of revision following cemented THA. While cemented femoral fixation remains a useful alternative for high-risk patients undergoing elective THA, the benefits may be compromised if the surgery is performed by surgeons whose specific volume for this type of fixation is low.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large retrospective cohort (n=1,970 patients) in Journal of Orthopaedic Trauma comparing PFNA versus TFNA cephalomedullary nails with a fivefold difference in mechanical failure rate, directly relevant to femoral fracture fixation practice.
bullets: Surgeons performing fewer than 60 cemented total hip stems over five years had twice the revision rate compared to higher-volume surgeons, with risk diverging within the first postoperative year.
Low-volume cemented stem surgeons also had significantly higher rates of periprosthetic fracture, loosening, infection, and dislocation at two-year follow-up.
Cemented femoral fixation remains a reasonable option for high-risk primary total hip arthroplasty patients, but outcomes depend heavily on surgeon-specific volume with this technique.

candidates.title: Radial Head Arthroplasty for Radial Head Fracture Is Associated with a Lower Rate of Reoperation Than Open Reduction Internal Fixation: A Population-Based Cohort Study.
candidates.authors_short: Carroll PJ, Chang N, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The purpose of this study was to (1) describe the longitudinal trends and epidemiology in surgical management of radial head fractures and (2) compare the rate of reoperation of open reduction internal fixation (ORIF) to radial head arthroplasty (RHA) in Ontario, Canada. METHODS: All patients aged 16 years and older who sustained a radial head fracture between April 1, 2002 and March 31, 2020 were identified using linked provincial health administrative databases from ICES. Patients undergoing ORIF, RHA or radial head excision for a radial head fracture were followed for subsequent reoperation. An unadjusted competing risk survival analysis was performed to tally the cumulative incidence of all-cause revision procedures. Logistic regression models were constructed to identify the patient-, provider- and fracture-related factors associated with reoperation following ORIF and RHA. RESULTS: A total of 3159 patients underwent surgical management of a radial head fracture during the study period. The majority of patients were female (55.9%). The mean age of patients who underwent ORIF, RHA and excision was 43.9, 51.1, 52.6 years, respectively. The mean (SD) follow-up times were 8.9 (+/- 5.0), 8.4 (+/- 5.0) and 11.0 (+/-5.0) years, respectively. In total, 7.7%, 3.8% and 0.8% experienced reoperation during study follow-up, respectively. At 10 years, the cumulative incidence function (CIF) for ORIF, RHA and excision was 15.8% (95% CI 13.9%-17.7%), 10.4% (95% CI 8.7%-12.3%) and 6.5% (95% CI 4.1%-9.5%), respectively. Gray's test demonstrated a statistically significant difference between groups favouring RHA over ORIF (P < 0.0001). The most frequently performed secondary procedure was removal of hardware (32%). The odds of reoperation among those younger than 40 years of age who had an ORIF increased when surgery was performed overnight (between midnight and 7AM) (P = 0.0008). CONCLUSION: Radial head arthroplasty was associated with a lower rate of reoperation than ORIF following radial head fractures, irrespective of patient age. Among patients younger than 40 years, overnight ORIF was associated with an increased rate of reoperation. Long-term studies are needed to evaluate the durability of these findings, particularly in younger patients. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, Retrospective Cohort Comparison using Large Database, Treatment Study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Prospective multicenter cohort (n=861 revision shoulder arthroplasties) in JSES developing an evidence-based predictive model for shoulder PJI diagnosis that directly challenges and refines the existing ICM consensus criteria.
bullets: In a population-based study of over 3,000 surgically treated radial head fractures, radial head arthroplasty had a 10-year reoperation rate of 10.4% compared to 15.8% for ORIF.
The reoperation advantage of arthroplasty over ORIF held regardless of patient age, with hardware removal being the most common reason for return to the operating room after ORIF.

In patients under 40 who underwent ORIF, surgery performed between midnight and 7am was independently associated with a higher rate of reoperation, suggesting timing of fixation matters in younger patients.

candidates.title: Predictive Modeling of Clinically Apparent Shoulder Periprosthetic Joint Infection (PJI).
candidates.authors_short: Hsu JE, Ricchetti ET, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The first International Consensus Meeting (ICM) definition of shoulder periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) introduced a tiered framework of PJI categories based on weighting of minor criteria for those cases not having major criteria of Definite infection. The selection of minor criteria and weightings was based on expert opinion and limited available evidence. The purpose of this study was to use prospective, multicenter data to develop a predictive model for clinically apparent shoulder PJI to inform a more evidence-based understanding of minor criteria and PJI categories. METHODS: Prospective data were collected on 861 consecutive revision shoulder arthroplasty cases within the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) Revision Shoulder Arthroplasty and PJI Multicenter Research Group. Presence of a sinus tract communicating with the prosthesis and intra-articular purulence were identified as pathognomonic indicators of infection (major criteria) and used as the primary outcome for multivariable analysis. Logistic regression modeling was performed, with model specification guided by information criteria. Variable selection emphasized optimal model fit while balancing complexity, focusing on: (1) markers of host inflammatory response, (2) universally available and commonly utilized diagnostic tests, (3) minimizing the total number of variables, and (4) preserving model usability despite missing data. RESULTS: Among 861 cases, 97 shoulders (11%) met the outcome of interest (sinus tract or intra-articular purulence). The final model incorporated seven variables spanning clinical findings, laboratory values, imaging, intraoperative assessment, and microbiology. These variables were erythema, unexpected wound drainage, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or C-reactive protein (CRP), radiographic humeral osteolysis, synovial neutrophils ≥70% or positive frozen section (≥5 polymorphonuclear cells in ≥5 high-powered fields), intraoperative humeral loosening, and ≥2 positive cultures with the same organism. The apparent concordance statistic in the development cohort was 0.90 (95% CI 0.87-0.94). A nomogram was subsequently developed to estimate the probability of PJI, defined by the presence of a sinus tract or intra-articular purulence. CONCLUSION: Using prospective, multicenter data, this study proposes a seven-factor nomogram to estimate the probability of clinically apparent shoulder PJI. The model showed strong apparent discrimination for clinically apparent infection in the development cohort. External validation will be necessary to confirm performance, and consensus will be required to establish weighting and diagnostic thresholds for tiers of non-definite shoulder PJI.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large population-based cohort (n=3,159 surgical radial head fractures) in JSES with long mean follow-up (~9 years) comparing ORIF versus radial head arthroplasty reoperation rates, providing high-level evidence for a common operative decision.
bullets: A seven-variable model using erythema, wound drainage, elevated ESR or CRP, humeral osteolysis on imaging, synovial neutrophil percentage or frozen section, intraoperative humeral loosening, and two or more positive cultures accurately identified clinically apparent shoulder periprosthetic joint infection in 11% of 861 revision cases.
The model applies to patients undergoing revision shoulder arthroplasty and showed strong ability to discriminate infected from non-infected cases in the development cohort.

A nomogram built from these seven variables may give surgeons a more evidence-based tool for diagnosing shoulder periprosthetic joint infection, though external validation is still needed before routine clinical use.

candidates.title: The use of patellar tendon autograft and lateral meniscus repair are associated with loss of motion of the knee among female patients undergoing anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
candidates.authors_short: Dadoo S, Nash AE, et al.
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: To conduct a sex-stratified analysis of factors associated with subsequent surgery for loss of motion after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), including meniscus repair and graft type. METHODS: All individuals age ≥14 years who underwent primary ACLR between 2014 and 2021 were reviewed. Exclusion criteria included <6 months follow-up and concomitant meniscal root, multiligament, osteochondral or osteotomy procedures. The primary outcome was subsequent surgery for loss of motion. Demographic and surgical variables were compared between individuals who underwent subsequent surgery for loss of motion versus not, for the full cohort and among females and males separately. Significance was set to p < 0.050. RESULTS: A total of 1226 individuals (age: 25 ± 10 years; 49% female) were included at a mean follow-up of 2.3 years. The rate of subsequent surgery for loss of motion was 9.0% for the full cohort, 12.3% for females and 5.9% for males. Among the full cohort, female sex (OR: 2.31; p < 0.001) and lateral meniscus (LM) repair (OR: 1.62; p = 0.048) were predictors of subsequent surgery for loss of motion. Among females, bone-patellar tendon-bone (BPTB) autograft use (OR: 1.91; p = 0.034) and LM repair (OR: 1.72; p = 0.046) were predictors of subsequent surgery for loss of motion, with combined BPTB autograft use and LM repair resulting in a significantly higher rate of subsequent surgery for loss of motion (32% vs. 12%; p = 0.004). Among males, graft type and meniscus repair were not associated with subsequent surgery for loss of motion (both p > 0.050). CONCLUSION: In this sex-stratified analysis, BPTB autograft use and LM repair were identified as factors predictive of subsequent surgery for loss of motion after primary ACLR when analysing females independently, while no predictive factors were identified when analysing males independently. Understanding factors associated with loss of motion after primary ACLR among males and females separately may guide individualised surgical decision-making and patient counselling. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective cohort study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Prospective RCT (n=68) in Foot & Ankle International directly comparing immediate weightbearing versus non-weightbearing after first MTP arthrodesis, addressing a practice-variation question with patient-centered outcomes at 12 months.
bullets: In female ACL reconstruction patients, patellar tendon autograft and lateral meniscus repair each independently increase the risk of subsequent surgery for stiffness, and combining both raises that rate from 12% to 32%.

Female sex carries roughly twice the risk of stiffness-related reoperation after ACL reconstruction compared to males, who show no significant association between graft type or meniscus repair and loss of motion.
When planning ACL reconstruction in female patients, surgeons should factor in the added stiffness risk before choosing patellar tendon autograft in cases that also require lateral meniscus repair.

candidates.title: Defining Long-Term Success After Anatomic Total Shoulder Arthroplasty: Survivorship and Clinically Important Outcomes.
candidates.authors_short: Kucharik MP, Hung V, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Long-term success after anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty (aTSA) is frequently defined by implant survivorship, but revision-free survival may not reflect durable clinical benefit. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study of 791 consecutive aTSAs performed between 2003 and 2015 was conducted. Implant survivorship was assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Clinical outcomes were evaluated at a 10-year landmark, and clinically important thresholds for the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) score were derived using patient satisfaction as the anchor. Multivariable regression identified predictors of revision and substantial clinical benefit (SCB). RESULTS: Kaplan-Meier survivorship was 96.1% at 10 years and 93.7% at 15 years. Walch B glenoid morphology and younger age were independently associated with revision. Clinical outcomes remained improved at long-term follow-up despite gradual attenuation over time. At 10 years, the patient acceptable symptom state (PASS) threshold for the ASES score was 68.1, and 69.5% of shoulders achieved it. The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) and SCB thresholds for the change in ASES score were 14.0 and 39.2, achieved by 79.9% and 55.8% of shoulders, respectively. Younger age, primary glenohumeral osteoarthritis, and lower preoperative ASES score were independently associated with achievement of SCB. CONCLUSIONS: aTSA demonstrated excellent long-term implant survivorship and modest patient-reported outcomes, although shoulder function gradually attenuated over extended follow-up. Despite the gradual functional decline, most patients maintained clinically meaningful benefit at 10 years. Younger age and Walch B morphology increased revision risk. Long-term clinically important thresholds provide patient-centered benchmarks for defining durable success. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic Level III. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.
candidates.score_reasoning: Prospective comparative cohort in Journal of Arthroplasty evaluating intrawound vancomycin powder safety in TKA (n=260) with serum level and renal outcome data, directly addressing a widely adopted but variably evidenced infection prophylaxis practice.
bullets: Anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty showed 96% implant survival at 10 years and 94% at 15 years, but meaningful functional gains gradually declined over that period.
At 10 years, about 70% of patients met an acceptable symptom threshold and 56% achieved substantial clinical benefit, with younger patients and those with worse preoperative function faring better.
Younger age and Walch B glenoid morphology independently increased revision risk, giving surgeons concrete preoperative factors to counsel patients about long-term expectations.
